title: Adobe Ends Free Creative Cloud Subscriptions for Stock Photographers
summary: Adobe ends free Creative Cloud subscriptions for stock photographers
detailed: Adobe is terminating its longstanding program that provided complimentary Creative Cloud subscriptions to stock photographers based on sales volume.

The free subscription scheme is being replaced by tier-based discounts, including a 70% discount on Creative Cloud Pro for the first 500 contributors meeting download and content-submission quotas or maintaining 10 or more datasets, and a 40% discount for up to 10,000 contributors meeting lower thresholds.

The new criteria apply to activities between September 22, 2026, and March 12, 2027, with discount codes distributed in April, while full complimentary access will continue only for actively commissioned content creators.

The change matters because it alters the economic incentives for contributors on Adobe Stock, replacing a popular non-monetary perk with discounted pricing structures that industry commentators view as a cost-cutting measure tied to AI data sourcing.
sentences: Adobe will no longer offer complimentary Creative Cloud subscriptions to photographers who sell their work through Adobe Stock, replacing the scheme with discounts instead.
For years, Adobe has incentivized photographers to contribute to its picture marketplace by dangling the carrot of a free subscription to Photoshop and other Adobe apps.

Robert Kneschke, a professional stock photographer based in Germany who runs the Daily Life of a Photo Producer blog, says that in 2020, a photographer needed 150 sales to unlock a free Adobe Photography plan, while 5,000 downloads would net them complete access to Creative Cloud.
But Adobe has recently made changes to its bonus program, changing the eligibility and prizes.
Instead of offering full complimentary access, Adobe is offering a 70% discount on Creative Cloud Pro to the first 500 contributors who generate 6,500 downloads and submit over 1,000 new images.

The 70% discount is also on offer to the first 500 contributors who “have 10 or more datasets and maintain high quality standards.” It’s not entirely clear what a dataset is from a photographer’s perspective.
The codes will be handed out in April.

Adobe will still provide full complimentary access to Creative Cloud Pro to photographers who are “actively commissioned to create content and/or require Adobe tools to fulfill project requirements.”
Writing on his blog, Kneschke calls the changes a “clear step backward” while speculating that the datasets are for AI training purposes.
“A gift has become a discount voucher,” Kneschke says.

“Along with the lower royalties, this is further evidence that Adobe is cutting costs at the expense of photographers.”
Earlier this year, PetaPixel reported on Gerald Carter, the owner of Diversity Photos, and his fight with Adobe after he discovered that the company trained its AI image generator Firefly on his entire photo library.
